candidates.text: She set it on the table where the post had lain all morning and did not open it for a long while. The envelope was soft as cloth, the postmark faded to a rust-coloured ghost of the town she had left at nineteen, the stamp a commemorative issue nobody had wanted. Inside, the ticket had gone the colour of old tea, but the date was still legible: the 7:40 to Ardmore, the fifteenth of September — thirty years from tomorrow. On the back, in the same hand that had addressed the envelope to a name she had not used in three decades, someone had pencilled a seat number, 31, the window, and beneath it a single word: *wait*.

The envelope was postmarked yesterday, which was the first oddity; the ticket inside was dated tomorrow. A single fare, Route 47, Ardmore Cross to the Central Terminus, valid for one journey only, the price printed in a currency that had not been legal tender for thirty years. The paper had gone the colour of weak tea, but the ink was black and fresh as if it had been struck this morning. I turned it over. On the back, in the same crisp hand, the date again, and beneath it four words in my own handwriting: *Wait at the stop. Don't wave.* I hadn't been to Ardmore Cross since I was nine years old. The stop had been pulled up in 2003 and replaced by a shelter on the far side of the overpass, and Route 47 had been renumbered twice and truncated in 2011; there was no 47 on any timetable now, and no Ardmore Cross at all. I checked the app twice, in case I had misremembered the road. Nothing. But a ticket, in my experience, is not an invitation — it is an instruction, and it does not care whether you have kept the appointment all this time. So I put it in my coat pocket. At ten to nine the next morning I stood on the far side of the overpass where the old stop had been, with the fog coming down off the river and my hands in my pockets, and I did not wave. At nine exactly a bus came round the corner that I did not recognise: no number on the front, no destination blind, windows opaque with steam, the doors sighing open like something waking up. The driver looked at me, and at the ticket in my hand, and nodded as though he had been expecting me for a very long time.

The envelope was addressed in my own handwriting, which was the first thing that put me wrong about it — the loop of my capital A leaning hard to the right, the way I signed my name before I was old enough to sign anything properly. The postmark was thirty years old, a faded blue ghost of the sorting office at Mill Lane, but the ticket inside was crisp as a brand-new one, the card still pale, the ink still wet-looking. Route 47. Fare 37p. Date: tomorrow. I turned it over, and on the back, in the printer's small type, the destination read WHITFIELD GATE, a stop that had been demolished before I was born. The timetable in my pocket — the one I had been meaning to replace since spring — confirmed what I already knew: no 47 ran to Whitfield Gate, or anywhere now. So I stood in the hall holding this small bright rectangle of paper, feeling its faint dampness, its impossible newness, and I understood that the seat had been booked, that someone in this city was keeping it warm, and that they expected me to be there. Outside, the evening traffic thinned, and somewhere down the road an engine turned over — a sound like a bus pulling away from a stop it had no intention of leaving.

instruction: Answer the brief as you normally would.

task.brief: A bus ticket bought thirty years ago arrives in the post, dated tomorrow. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the ticket forces a small concrete decision
the paragraph makes the elapsed thirty years felt without explaining them
the ending leaves the reader uneasy rather than resolved
task.reference_text: The envelope had been forwarded twice and the postmark was this morning's. Inside, the ticket was warm, as though it had been held, and the destination printed on it was the town she had left at nineteen without telling anyone she was going.
